extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers, economists, and policymakers studying mortgage markets, fintech lending, and shadow banking
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical economics paper measuring differences between traditional banks, shadow banks, and fintech lenders in mortgage origination, pricing, financing, and performance; uses HMDA and GSE data with county- and loan-level regressions. Focuses on linking shadow bank growth to regulatory changes between 2007–2015.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of originator type (traditional / shadow / fintech)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicator variables for originator type: an indicator taking value 1 (the text shows 100 in notation) if the originator is a shadow bank (or fintech shadow bank) and 0 otherwise; regressions are run both on the full sample (shadow vs non-shadow) and within shadow banks (fintech vs non-fintech).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use HMDA for broad market coverage and Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac data for more detailed credit/term info. Apply this classification consistently across loan-level and market-level specifications; note HMDA limitations (e.g., conforming classification only if sold same calendar year).

rubrics_metrics.name: Time_to_Sale metric (originator holding period)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define Time_to_Sale for borrower i of lender type j at location z at time t in units of quarters (mean roughly 40 days). Regression: Time_to_Sale = function(bank_type_dummy, loan_controls, zip-time fixed effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret shorter time-to-sale for shadow banks as evidence of limited balance sheet capacity; compare coefficients in quarters (e.g., 0.10 quarters ≈ 9 days). Control for loan characteristics and zip-time fixed effects to compare within market and time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual-level linear probability model for originator type
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification where the dependent variable is an indicator that a residential mortgage was originated by a shadow bank (or, within shadow banks, by a fintech). The model includes borrower and loan characteristics (income, race, loan purpose, loan type) and county x time fixed effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coefficients are in percentage points. Estimate separately using HMDA and GSE data; HMDA gives broader coverage (race, financing), GSE data gives detailed credit (FICO, LTV) but limited to FRM loans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market-level (county) regression of shadow bank penetration
rubrics_metrics.description: Regression of 2015 shadow bank market share (and fintech share of shadow bank loans) on county characteristics: % minority, unemployment, education, lending concentration, and other demographics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use county x time comparisons and weighted least squares with weights = 2008 originations. Present both average differences and regression-adjusted results. Use county fixed effects or controls to separate within-market changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loan pricing regression (mortgage interest rate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependent variable: mortgage interest rate in percentage points. Key regressors: dummies for non-fintech shadow bank and fintech shadow bank; controls include borrower FICO, loan-to-value, debt-to-income and zip code x quarter fixed effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Zip-quarter fixed effects absorb supply/demand/regulatory differences across markets. Interpret coefficients in basis points (e.g., fintech charged ~13 bps more than traditional banks). Control for observable borrower/loan characteristics to compare 'observationally equivalent borrowers.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Loan performance metrics: default and prepayment
rubrics_metrics.description: Default: indicator for being at least 60 days delinquent within two years of origination. Prepayment: analogous indicator measuring prepayment within two years. Regressions control for mortgage rate, borrower and mortgage characteristics, and zip-quarter fixed effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrict sample to loans with two years of performance (e.g., originate 2010–2013). Use these metrics to compare ex-post risk (default) and prepayment behavior across lender types; interpret magnitudes relative to base rates (e.g., ~11% two-year prepayment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Financing-source share metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure shares of originated mortgages by financing source: held on balance sheet vs sold (to GSEs, insurance companies, affiliates, private securitization), and track changes over time and across lender types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for HMDA recording conventions (loans not sold within calendar year are recorded as not sold). Use Fannie/Freddie data where date-of-sale is observed to correct for timing misclassification (e.g., ~9% sold in different year). Compare trends across 2007–2015 and across lender types (traditional, shadow, fintech).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of county-level capital requirement exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute change in individual bank's tier 1 risk-based capital ratio from 2008 to 2015 and aggregate to county level by weighting banks by their share of the county mortgage market in 2008: county_change = 100 * (weighted sum of bank-level changes) / (weighted base).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this county-level Δ(tier1) as a measure of regulatory pressure from capital requirements. Hypothesis: counties with larger increases saw larger shadow bank market share gains. Standardize this measure by its cross-sectional standard deviation when included in regressions for comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of county-level MSR exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute origination-weighted mortgage servicing rights (MSR) as percent of tier 1 capital at county level: MSR%r = 100 * (sum MSR_s / sum tier1_capital) weighted by 2008 originations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pre-existing MSR reliance to proxy which counties faced higher regulatory cost of servicing after Basel III changes. Hypothesis: higher MSR exposure counties saw greater shadow bank gains. Standardize by cross-sectional sd for regression comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of county-level lawsuit exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregate accumulated mortgage lawsuit settlements for banks (2008–2015) to county exposure by weighting each bank's settlements by its share of 2008 county lending: county_lawsuit_exposure = 100 * (weighted sum of settlements) / (weighted base).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exposure as a proxy for increased legal/regulatory scrutiny affecting traditional banks. Hypothesis: counties with greater exposure saw larger shadow bank market share and lending growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of county-level OTS exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the county share of originations in 2008 that were regulated by the Office of Thrift Supervision (OTS): OTS%r = 100 * (OTS_regulated_originations / total_originations) in 2008.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a shock variable for the effect of the OTS dissolution (2011). Hypothesis: counties with higher pre-2011 OTS share saw greater shadow bank growth after its closure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome variables for regulation difference-in-difference tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Two outcomes: (1) change in shadow bank market share between 2008 and 2015 (percent change); (2) growth in shadow bank lending between 2008 and 2015 as a share of 2008 lending. Formulas provided in text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run regressions Δ(shadow_share) = α + β * Regulation_r + X_c + ε and Δ(shadow_lending) = α + β * Regulation_r + X_c + ε, where Regulation_r is one of the standardized county-level regulatory measures. Weight regressions by 2008 originations (WLS). Include county controls (demographics, 2008 bank share).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardization and weighting conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Standardize regulation measures by dividing by the cross-sectional standard deviation so coefficients represent percent changes per one sd. Use weighted least squares regressions weighted by 2008 originations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standardization facilitates comparison across different regulatory measures. Weighting by 2008 originations accounts for heterogeneity in county lending volumes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of zip-code x quarter (or county x time) fixed effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Include zip x quarter fixed effects in loan-level pricing and performance regressions (and county x time in other specs) to absorb local supply/demand/regulatory conditions and compare 'observationally equivalent' borrowers within market and time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixed effects are critical to isolate lender-type effects from market-level heterogeneity. Use when comparing rates and performance within the same geographic/time market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data choice tradeoffs: HMDA vs Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac
rubrics_metrics.description: HMDA offers broader coverage and variables like borrower race and financing indicator but has limitations (e.g., conforming classification only if sold same calendar year). Fannie/Freddie data are narrower (mostly FRM) but include detailed credit info (FICO, LTV) and date-of-sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use HMDA for broad market patterns and race/financing analyses; use GSE data for detailed credit-quality and term-based analyses and to correct for HMDA timing biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample restrictions for performance analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrict loans to those with two years of available performance to measure default (>=60 days delinquent within two years) and prepayment; this typically limits the sample to loans originated between 2010 and 2013 for the studied window.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure comparable follow-up windows when comparing performance across lender types to avoid bias from differential seasoning or observation windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation guidance for small effect sizes
rubrics_metrics.description: When effect sizes are small in absolute terms (e.g., shadow bank default rates ~0.02% higher translating to ~3 FICO points), contextualize magnitudes relative to baseline rates and economic significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report both statistical and economic significance; compare percentage-point differences to relevant scales (e.g., basis points for interest rates, percentiles or points for FICO).
